chunks: As for your saying: 'We are both sons of 'Abd Manaf,' it is so, we are.
But Umayyah is not like Hashim, nor Harb like 'Abd al-Muttalib, nor Abu Sufyan like Abu Talib.

Nor the immigrant (Mu'awiya) is like the one set free (Zubayr), nor the pure (by lineage) like the adopted (by status), nor the pursuer of truth like the adherent to wrong, nor the believer like the hypocrite.
And how bad a successor is one who follows predecessors who have fallen in the fire of Hell.

key_terms.أُمَيَّةُ: Umayyah, father of the Umayyad clan
key_terms.السَّلَف: The predecessors, referring to earlier generations or forefathers
key_terms.الطَّلِيقُ: The one set free, referring to Zubayr ibn al-Awwam who was freed from slavery
key_terms.الْمُهَاجِرُ: The immigrant, referring to Mu'awiya ibn Abi Sufyan
key_terms.عَبْدُ مَنَافٍ: Abd Manaf, the common ancestor of the Prophet's family and the Umayyads
key_terms.هَاشِمٌ: Hashim, grandfather of the Prophet, known for high status

ai.seo_question: How does Imam Ali distinguish the nobility of the Prophet's family from the Umayyads in his letter to Muawiya?
ai.summary: Imam Ali (peace be upon him) refutes Mu'awiya’s claim to superiority based solely on Qurayshi lineage by distinguishing between *nasab* (genealogy) and *fadilah* (virtue), asserting that Hashim and Abd al-Muttalib were superior to Umayyah and Harb due to their piety and leadership. The rhetorical contrasts, such as 'the migrator' (Mu'awiya) versus 'the free' (Zubayr) and 'the clear' versus 'the sticky', highlight the qualitative difference between the Ahl al-Bayt and the Umayyads, emphasizing that true nobility lies in faith and character rather than mere ancestry. This passage underscores the Shia scholarly principle that lineage is only a means to an end if accompanied by righteousness, warning against those who follow predecessors who fell into Hellfire.
